questions.q: What is the core distinction between DECIMAL/NUMERIC and FLOAT/REAL on SQL Server?
options: DECIMAL/NUMERIC are exact; FLOAT/REAL are approximate IEEE 754 binary floating-point
DECIMAL/NUMERIC are deprecated in favor of FLOAT/REAL
They are interchangeable aliases for the same storage format
FLOAT/REAL are exact and DECIMAL/NUMERIC are approximate
questions.explain: DECIMAL/NUMERIC store exact fixed-precision values, while FLOAT/REAL are approximate binary floating-point.

questions.q: How do MySQL and PostgreSQL's numeric type families compare to SQL Server's?
options: They follow the same two-family pattern: exact DECIMAL/NUMERIC and approximate FLOAT/DOUBLE
They have no exact numeric type at all
They only support floating-point numbers, with no exact decimal type
They use Oracle's single NUMBER type instead of separate families
questions.explain: MySQL and PostgreSQL both have the same exact-vs-approximate split as SQL Server.

questions.q: What is distinctive about Oracle's NUMBER type?
options: It's a single flexible type, using precision and scale, that can represent both integer-like and decimal values
Oracle has no numeric type and requires VARCHAR2 for all numbers
NUMBER is only usable for approximate floating-point values
NUMBER is identical to SQL Server's INT and cannot store decimals
questions.explain: NUMBER(precision, scale) covers what SQL Server splits across INT, DECIMAL, and more, through one flexible type.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is using FLOAT/REAL/DOUBLE for money a platform-specific mistake or a universal one?
options: It's wrong on every platform in this course, because IEEE 754 floating-point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly
It's only a mistake in Oracle, since other platforms handle floating-point money correctly
It's actually the recommended approach for money on every platform
It's only a mistake in SQL Server, since other platforms don't have floating-point types
questions.explain: Floating-point imprecision for money is a universal issue across every platform covered in this course, not a single-vendor quirk.

questions.q: In Oracle, how would you declare a column that behaves like a simple integer using NUMBER?
options: NUMBER(10) with scale 0 or omitted
NUMBER(10, 2), always with a nonzero scale
It's impossible -- Oracle has no way to represent integers
FLOAT(10), since integers must use approximate types in Oracle
questions.explain: A NUMBER column with scale 0 or omitted behaves like an integer; a positive scale makes it behave like a fixed-point decimal.
